primary_topics: Chapter 13 of 'With Due Respect' (Vol. 7) -- CJP's March 18, 2007 Inquirer column explaining why the Catholic Bishops' Conference of the Philippines (CBCP) does not endorse candidates, tracing the Church's political engagement to the Second Vatican Council

How Vatican II's call for the laity's 'total or integral development' and the 'empowerment of the faithful' transformed the Church into one that is 'pro-life, pro-poor... pro-human rights' and urges the laity 'never to relinquish participation in public life'

The division of roles set by the Second Plenary Council of the Philippines (PCP II) Resolution 28 -- the laity to 'promote the election... of leaders of true integrity,' the clergy to 'refrain from partisan politics' -- and the autonomy of each bishop, answerable to Rome, not the CBCP

Why Archbishop Lagdameo rejected Bro. Mike Velarde's proposal to 'choose candidates,' the Church preferring to back the nonpartisan PPCRV's call for candidates of 'principles, programs and performance' over 'payoff, personality... and patronage' -- an indirect path CJP defends as wiser than 'confrontational' endorsement
sub_topics: The shift: 'prior to 1965, the Catholic Church's involvement in politics was largely unheard of,' but 'since then... Church militancy in political affairs has increasingly become visible and audible' -- a change CJP traces to the Second Vatican Council (1962-1965)

Integral development: Vatican II 'underscored the need for the Christians' total or integral development,' so believers must 'act out their faith in all facets of their being' -- Christianity not 'merely sav[ing] souls for the next life' but liberating people to develop 'spiritually, economically, socially, culturally, and politically,' making the Church 'pro-life, pro-poor, pro-environment, pro-human rights, and pro-principle'

The laity's mandate: a Vatican II-era document, 'Christifideles Laici,' asked the lay faithful 'never to relinquish participation in public life,' encouraging qualified Christians to 'restore all things in Christ' -- and 'Lumen Gentium' proclaimed 'the empowerment of the faithful' and their equality 'in dignity and in mission' with the clergy, as 'co-workers,' not 'mere deputies'

PCP II Resolution 28: echoing Vatican II, the Second Plenary Council of the Philippines (Makati, 1991) -- the first to seat lay leaders in its 'lawmaking' body -- set out in Resolution 28 that the laity 'must help form the civic conscience' and 'promote the election... of leaders of true integrity,' while 'bishops, priests and religious... must refrain from partisan politics,' avoiding 'the use of the pulpit for partisan purposes to avoid division among the flock'
CJP as a witness: 'as a lay participant in PCP II,' CJP recalls 'quite vividly the emphasis given... to these distinct roles of the laity and the clergy'

Rome's prudence: the Holy See 'does not encourage direct clergy intervention in State or partisan affairs (like endorsing candidates),' since the Universal Church works in countries like 'China and Vietnam,' where its 'evangelization mission... would be hindered' if 'civil authorities... became suspicious of its pastoral activities'

The Velarde rejection: against this background, CBCP president Archbishop Angel Lagdameo 'rejected the proposal of Bro. Mike Velarde to choose candidates for the May 14 senatorial elections,' explaining that to 'dictate on [the faithful] whom to vote for is as bad as buying their votes' -- and noting that 'there is no national Catholic authority that can command such a choice,' each diocese being 'autonomous' and each bishop 'responsible directly to Rome, not... even to the CBCP'

The PPCRV alternative: bishops thus limit themselves to issuing 'guidelines' and support the nonpartisan Parish Pastoral Council for Responsible Voting (PPCRV), which -- in a call CJP likens to his own for 'visionary leaders by example' -- urges electing candidates of 'principles, programs and performance' and rejecting those of 'payoff, personality (or popularity) and patronage'; critics may call this 'indirect and extremely cautious,' but 'the direct and confrontational method may be short-sighted and harmful to both the Church and the State in the long term'

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 13 of 'With Due Respect' (Vol. 7), CJP's March 18, 2007 Inquirer column, explains why the CBCP does not endorse candidates. 'Prior to 1965,' he notes, 'the Catholic Church's involvement in politics was largely unheard of,' a change he traces to the Second Vatican Council (1962-1965), which 'underscored the need for the Christians' total or integral development' -- believers acting out their faith 'in all facets,' Christianity not 'merely sav[ing] souls for the next life' but liberating people to develop 'spiritually, economically, socially, culturally, and politically,' making the Church 'pro-life, pro-poor... pro-human rights.' A Vatican II-era document, 'Christifideles Laici,' asked the laity 'never to relinquish participation in public life,' and 'Lumen Gentium' proclaimed 'the empowerment of the faithful' as 'co-workers' equal 'in dignity and in mission.' Echoing this, the Second Plenary Council of the Philippines (1991) set out in Resolution 28 that the laity 'must... promote the election... of leaders of true integrity,' while 'bishops, priests and religious... must refrain from partisan politics,' avoiding 'the pulpit for partisan purposes.' The Holy See, CJP adds, 'does not encourage direct clergy intervention,' lest the Church's work in 'China and Vietnam' be hindered. So CBCP president Archbishop Lagdameo 'rejected the proposal of Bro. Mike Velarde to choose candidates for the May 14 senatorial elections,' since to 'dictate... whom to vote for is as bad as buying their votes,' and 'no national Catholic authority' can command a vote, each bishop being 'autonomous' and 'responsible directly to Rome.' Bishops thus issue only 'guidelines' and back the nonpartisan PPCRV's call -- akin to CJP's own for 'visionary leaders by example' -- for 'principles, programs and performance' over 'payoff, personality... and patronage'; this 'indirect and extremely cautious' path, he argues, is wiser than a 'confrontational method' that would harm 'both the Church and the State.'
